Banks aren't printing money in the way a counterfeiter does. They don't just produce money and say 'look this is ours, let's go spend it'. You're right, that would be very bad for everyone if they did.

When a bank loans to someone they create a liability on their own balance sheet and when you pay it back that liability gets cancelled out, the bank never has more money at any point (except from interest payments/fees etc.). The person who they loan the money to is the one who ends up with the extra money, it disappears again once it's repaid.

The idea is that as economic activity increases, more people will take out loans to facilitate it. So the money supply is kind of controlled by the economy itself. This is supposed to minimise inflation/deflation. If you just have a fixed pool of money then any fluctuation in economic activity is going to cause inflation or deflation of the value of the currency (the same amount of money to buy more or less stuff), if you have an elastic supply tied to the amount of economic activity (more money around to buy more stuff, less to buy less stuff) then it should help to combat inflation and deflation because it alters the amount of currency available rather than it's value.

Do you get it now? Altering the amount of money is a means to absorb the the impact of changes in the size of the economy to keep the value of money relatively stable.
